overview: These notes are for CISA holders preparing for The IIA's CIA Challenge Exam. Section by section, they show which CISA habits carry over, which words change and which rules are new, mostly in running the function, the board's part, quality and results. Each lesson is written in The IIA's terms; the CISA comparison sits apart, in a labeled table and one exam trap.
analogy: Think of an experienced airline pilot moving to a new aircraft type. Flying skill, checklists and radio discipline all carry over, so the type-rating course skips basic flying. It spends its hours on what differs: the new cockpit layout, different callouts for the same actions, and who in the crew does which task. A pilot who flies the new plane by the old plane's habits makes the costly mistakes.

subtopics.name: What Transfers and What Is New
subtopics.definition: The bridge map shows which CISA-trained habits carry over to The IIA's Challenge Exam, which need new words, and which topics are new ground.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most engagement skill carries over, so study time belongs where the exam is new to you: running the function, the board's part, quality and results.
how_it_works: Section A, 20%: mandate, independence, objectivity, confidentiality, quality and performance measures. New ground beyond the charter and independence basics.
Section B, 15%: methodologies, budget, people, strategy, the risk-based plan and other assurance providers. Almost all of it is new.
Section C, 20%: objectives, scope, criteria, engagement risk assessment, approach and resources. Planning transfers; the approvers and the vocabulary change.
Section D, 25%: evidence, analytics, findings, workpapers, conclusions, supervision and communication. The most familiar section; watch the evidence words and the conclusion.
Section E, 20%: final communication, action plans, residual risk, risk acceptance and follow-up. The steps transfer; approving, sending and escalating move to the chief audit executive.

subtopics.example: Teodora, an IT audit manager in Bucharest, books the Challenge Exam eight weeks out. She skims evidence and sampling, which she uses daily, and spends most evenings on board approvals, the quality program and risk acceptance. Each Sunday she checks her hours against the section weights and moves time to the section she scores lowest in.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Study by weight and by novelty: engagement skill mostly carries over, while running the function, reporting to the board, quality and risk acceptance are new. Answer every question in The IIA's words, from the seat it gives you.

exam_traps.trap: Years of IT audit mean Sections C and D need no study.
exam_traps.why: The steps transfer, but the words, the approvers and each rule's strength differ, and options in another body's wording target that habit.

exam_traps.trap: The option with the deepest IT control detail is the safest pick.
exam_traps.why: The exam asks what a fact means for the engagement or the function. IT detail is usually context; the best answer is an internal auditor's step.

subtopics.name: Three Seats, One Exam
subtopics.definition: A seat is the role a question puts you in: internal auditor, engagement supervisor or chief audit executive. Each seat approves, sends or escalates different things.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many wrong options describe a sound action taken by the wrong person.
how_it_works: Must: internal auditors plan, test, document, draft the final communication and confirm that actions were implemented (Standards 14.6, 15.1, 15.2).
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE), or a supervisor the CAE delegates to, approves objectives, scope, the work program and the documentation (Standards 13.3, 13.6, 14.6).
Must: the CAE approves the final communication, decides who receives it and seeks advice before any outside release (Standards 11.3, 15.1).
Must: the CAE takes matters to the board, such as an unresolved scope limitation or risk accepted beyond appetite (Standards 13.3, 11.5).
Must: supervision runs from planning to sign-off and its evidence is kept; the CAE may delegate it but stays accountable (Standard 12.3).

columns: On the CIA exam: who acts

rows.label: Issues the report
cells: The IS auditor, to the audit committee (CISA notes 1B5.3)
Internal auditors draft; the CAE approves and decides who receives it

rows.label: Approves a program change
cells: The manager, 'with approval'; the approver is not named (CISA notes 1B1.2)
The CAE, or a supervisor the CAE delegates to

rows.label: Goes to the board
cells: The IS auditor escalates to the audit committee (CISA notes 1B5.5)
The CAE; internal auditors go up through the supervisor to the CAE

subtopics.example: In a Lima water utility, auditor Rosa finds that the operations director has blocked access to pump-station maintenance logs. She asks him once more, documents the refusal and tells her engagement supervisor, who briefs chief audit executive Marta. Rosa does not write to the board herself.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Before choosing, name the seat. Internal auditors do and draft; the CAE, or a delegated supervisor, approves; the CAE alone sends results and takes matters to the board. A right action by the wrong person is a wrong answer.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor who found the problem should brief the board directly, because that is fastest.
exam_traps.why: Reaching the board is the CAE's step. The auditor documents the matter and takes it up the line for the CAE to judge.

exam_traps.trap: A delegated engagement supervisor's approval moves accountability for the work to that supervisor.
exam_traps.why: Delegation moves the task, not the accountability. The CAE still answers for the approval, the supervision and the final communication.

key_terms.definition: The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.
KaiSip's word for the role a question puts you in, which decides who approves, sends and escalates.

subtopics.memory_aid: Auditors do and draft; the CAE approves, sends and escalates.

subtopics.name: Must, Should and Essential Conditions
subtopics.definition: Strength is how binding a line of the Standards is: Requirements say must, Considerations for Implementation say should or may, and essential conditions describe the board's part.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many options differ only in strength. Turning a should into a must, or putting a must on the board, marks the trap.
how_it_works: Must: each standard's Requirements bind internal auditors and the chief audit executive (CAE); conformance means meeting them.
Should or may: Considerations for Implementation describe preferred or optional practice; an answer resting on one says 'should' or 'leading practice', never 'must'.
Essential conditions: what the board and senior management do for an effective function, listed in Domain III; they are not requirements the CAE can enforce.
Must: when the board or senior management disagrees with an essential condition, the CAE shows its impact with examples; should: discuss alternatives (Domain III).
Syllabus only: lines such as mission statements or job design rest on the syllabus alone; learn them as common usage, never as a must.

rows.label: Binding layer
cells: ITAF standards, a floor with no departure (CISA notes 1A1.1)
Requirements: must

rows.label: Advisory layer
cells: ITAF guidelines: consider them, justify any departure
Considerations for Implementation: should or may

rows.label: The board's part
cells: The audit committee approves and oversees (CISA notes 1A1.4)
Essential conditions: what the board does, not rules on it

rows.label: A rule you cannot meet
cells: Never set aside, whatever the reason
Nonconformance, documented and disclosed (Standard 4.1)

subtopics.example: In Auckland, the audit committee chair tells chief audit executive Aroha that private sessions with her will stop. Aroha cannot order the board to meet her. She explains, with two recent examples, what the sessions protect, suggests a shorter session, and records the decision and her concern.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Read the verb before the content. Must binds the auditor or the CAE; should and may are leading or optional practice; the board's duties are essential conditions the CAE discusses, explains and documents. Match the option's strength to the Standard's.

exam_traps.trap: When the board drops an essential condition, the CAE reports the board's nonconformance with the Standards.
exam_traps.why: Essential conditions do not bind the board. The CAE shows the impact and documents the outcome; without agreement, the CAE may conclude the function cannot conform.

exam_traps.trap: An option calling CEO reporting mandatory is the strongest answer, since independence matters most.
exam_traps.why: Standard 7.1 calls administrative reporting to the chief executive officer (CEO) leading practice, a should. A 'must' version of a should is the wrong option.

key_terms.definition: A 'must' in a standard: mandatory.
A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.

subtopics.memory_aid: Must binds you; should guides you; essential conditions describe the board.

subtopics.name: The Board and Senior Management
subtopics.definition: The board is the highest governing body, often acting through an audit committee; senior management is the top executive team. The Standards give the two different jobs.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Options that join them, such as 'senior management and the board approve', sound safe and are often wrong.
how_it_works: Essential condition: the board approves the charter, the plan, the budget and the resource plan (Standard 6.3). Must: significant plan changes also need its approval (Standard 9.4).
Essential condition: senior management supports the function, helps secure its access, and works with the board to provide resources (Standards 6.3, 8.2).
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) discusses the charter and the plan with both, takes input from both, and reports results to both (Standards 6.2, 9.4, 11.3).
Must: the internal audit strategy is reviewed with both periodically; the Standards ask for review, not approval (Standard 9.2).
Essential condition: the board authorizes the CAE's appointment and removal and gives senior management input on the CAE's pay and evaluation (Standard 7.1).

rows.label: Who oversees audit
cells: The audit committee (CISA notes 1A1.4)
The board, which may be an audit committee

rows.label: Approves the plan
cells: The audit committee (CISA notes 1A3.1)
The board alone, after discussion with both

rows.label: Senior management's part
cells: An administrative line and copies of reports (CISA notes 1A1.3, CISA notes 1B5.3)

subtopics.example: At a Nairobi insurer, the chief executive officer asks chief audit executive Wanjiru to send him the revised audit plan for sign-off before the audit committee meets. Wanjiru discusses the plan with him and adds two risks he raises, then presents it to the committee for approval.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The board approves and oversees; senior management informs, supports and helps resource the function. The CAE discusses with both and reports to both. When an option has senior management approving the charter or the plan, look again.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management and the board jointly approve the internal audit plan.
exam_traps.why: The CAE discusses the plan with both, but approval of the plan, and of each significant change to it, belongs to the board (Standard 9.4).

exam_traps.trap: The board sets the CAE's pay, because the CAE reports to it.
exam_traps.why: The board authorizes appointment and removal and gives senior management input on pay and evaluation (Standard 7.1). The Standards do not say the board sets the pay.

key_terms.definition: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.

subtopics.memory_aid: Board approves; senior management supports; the CAE talks to both.

subtopics.name: Words That Change
subtopics.definition: Word swaps are terms that mean nearly the same in KaiSip's CISA notes and in The IIA's Standards; only The IIA's term belongs in a CIA answer.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The CIA exams are written in The IIA's 2024 vocabulary. A familiar word from CISA study can mark a distractor, or hide a rule that works differently.
how_it_works: Roles: internal auditor, engagement supervisor, chief audit executive, board, senior management, and the people who manage the activity under review.
Documents: the internal audit charter holding the mandate, the internal audit plan, the work program, workpapers and the final communication.
Evidence and results: relevant, reliable and sufficient information; significance; findings; an engagement conclusion rather than an opinion.
Services: assurance services and advisory services. The Standards use 'advisory', and a CIA answer should too.
Follow-up: confirming that recommendations or action plans were implemented, by a set method scaled to significance (Standard 15.2).

'The audit committee approves the annual plan' becomes 'the board approves the internal audit plan'; 'auditee' becomes 'the management of the activity under review'. He drills the new cards until the old words stop coming first.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Answer in The IIA's 2024 words: internal auditor, board, activity under review, work program, action plan, engagement conclusion. When an option speaks another body's language, check whether its rule is The IIA's too.

exam_traps.trap: 'IS auditor' and 'internal auditor' mean the same thing on the CIA exams.
exam_traps.why: The internal auditor's remit is all of governance, risk management and control, not only information systems. The CIA exams use only The IIA's term.

key_terms.definition: The area, process, system or unit that an engagement examines.
Management's stated steps to deal with a finding, with a named owner and a target date.
The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.

subtopics.memory_aid: New exam, new words: board, activity under review, work program, action plan.

topics.topic_name: Professionalism and quality, coming from CISA
topics.overview: Section A starts from ideas a CISA holder knows, the charter, independence and objectivity, then goes further: where authority comes from, roles beyond internal auditing, the quality program, and what happens when a standard cannot be met.
can_do: Explain who sets the mandate and who approves the charter
Apply the 12-month presumption and the route for disclosing an impairment
Describe the safeguards for roles beyond internal auditing
Describe what the board approves and receives in the quality program

subtopics.name: Mandate and Charter
subtopics.definition: The internal audit mandate is the function's authority, role and responsibilities; the internal audit charter records it, and the board approves the charter.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Authority that management could withdraw is not independent. Knowing where the mandate comes from, and who approves the charter, settles many Section A questions.
how_it_works: Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) gives the board and senior management the information needed to set the mandate, then documents it in the charter (Standards 6.1, 6.2).
The mandate may come from the board, from laws and regulations, or both; the CAE never grants it.
Must: the CAE develops the charter, discusses the draft with the board and senior management, and keeps it current (Standard 6.2).
Essential condition: the board approves the charter; senior management gives input and never approves it (Standards 6.2, 6.3).
Must: the charter covers at least the purpose, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate, and the function's position and reporting lines (Standard 6.2).

columns: On the CIA exam: the charter

rows.label: Source of authority
cells: The charter itself (CISA notes 1A1.3)
The mandate, from the board, law or both; the charter holds it

rows.label: Approver
cells: Board or audit committee, or the highest level of management without one
The board, as the Standards define it

rows.label: Senior management
cells: An administrative line (CISA notes 1A1.3)
Gives input on the draft; does not approve

subtopics.example: At a Manila logistics firm, a new regulation requires internal audit to review customs filings every year. Chief audit executive Carmela tells the board and senior management what the law now requires, drafts the charter change, discusses it with both, and takes it to the board for approval.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The mandate is authority, role and responsibilities, from the board, from law or both; the charter records it. The CAE informs, drafts and discusses; the board approves. Senior management's input never becomes approval.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, the charter itself grants internal audit its authority.
exam_traps.why: On the CIA exam the authority is the mandate, given by the board, by law or both. The charter documents it; the CAE never grants it.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE approves the charter, because the CAE wrote it.
exam_traps.why: The CAE develops and maintains the charter, but the board approves it (Standard 6.2). Drafting is not approving.

key_terms.definition: What the function may do, the part it plays and what it must deliver; set by the board, by law, or both.
The board-approved document holding the function's mandate, position and reporting lines.

subtopics.memory_aid: Mandate is the power, charter is the paper, and the board approves it.

subtopics.name: Independence of the Function
subtopics.definition: Independence belongs to the internal audit function and comes from its direct reporting line to the board; the chief audit executive confirms it to the board yearly.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A sound reporting line is only the start. The chief audit executive keeps confirming independence and acts when budget, scope or access is squeezed.
how_it_works: Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) confirms the function's independence to the board at least yearly, with any incidents and the safeguards used (Standard 7.1).
Essential condition: the board keeps a direct reporting line with the CAE and authorizes the CAE's appointment and removal (Standard 7.1).
Should: reporting administratively to the chief executive officer is leading practice; another senior officer can serve with safeguards (Standard 7.1).
May impair independence: management limiting approved scope, restricting access, pressing to change findings, or cutting the budget below what the charter needs (Standard 7.1).
Must: when money falls short, the CAE promptly tells the board and senior management the impact (Standard 10.1).

rows.label: Main safeguard
cells: A functional line to the audit committee (CISA notes 1A1.3, CISA notes 1A1.5)
A direct line to the board, plus a yearly confirmation

rows.label: Administrative line
cells: Usually senior management
The chief executive officer as leading practice, a should

rows.label: Budget squeeze
cells: Re-rank by risk and brief the committee (CISA notes 1B1.4)
May impair independence; the impact is reported promptly

subtopics.example: In Rotterdam, chief audit executive Pieter reports administratively to the chief financial officer. Soon after his team starts reviewing treasury, which also reports to her, she cuts the audit budget by a third. Pieter tells the board and senior management what coverage the cut removes and raises the independence concern privately with the board.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence belongs to the function and comes from its position. Confirm it to the board yearly, report incidents and safeguards, and treat cuts to budget, scope or access as possible impairments the board and senior management hear about promptly.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, once the function reports to an audit committee, independence needs nothing more.
exam_traps.why: The CAE must still confirm independence to the board at least yearly, with incidents and safeguards. A sound line does not stop budget, scope or access pressure.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require administrative reporting to the chief executive officer.
exam_traps.why: Standard 7.1 calls it leading practice, a should. Another senior officer may serve when safeguards are in place.

key_terms.definition: The function's freedom, gained from its position, to do and report its work without being steered by those it audits.
The chief audit executive's direct reporting line to the board.
The chief audit executive's day-to-day line to a member of management, ideally the chief executive officer.

subtopics.memory_aid: A line to the board, a yearly confirmation, a prompt warning when squeezed.

subtopics.name: The Person: Objectivity and Confidentiality
subtopics.definition: Objectivity is each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind; confidentiality means using engagement information only for the work and sharing it only as allowed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Objectivity is judged person by person. Fixed rules on former responsibilities and a disclosure route that depends on the seat decide many questions.
how_it_works: Must: never assess a specific activity you were responsible for; for assurance, objectivity is presumed impaired if that ended within 12 months (Standard 2.2).
Must: assurance after advisory work on the same area needs the chief audit executive's (CAE's) confirmation that objectivity holds, and suitable staffing (Standard 2.2).
Must: disclose an impairment to a designated supervisor or the CAE; the CAE's own impairment goes to the board (Standard 2.3).
May: reassign, reschedule, adjust the scope or outsource the work; the Standards rank none of these remedies (Standard 2.3).
Must: use information only as policy and law allow, never for gain, and disclose it only when authorized or under a legal or professional duty (Standards 5.1, 5.2).

cells: A cooling-off period, judged case by case (CISA notes 1A1.5)
Never assess it; presumed impaired for assurance within 12 months

rows.label: Who hears it
cells: Audit management (CISA notes 1A1.5)
A designated supervisor or the CAE; the CAE's own goes to the board

Options with no ranking; the CAE decides

subtopics.example: Lindiwe joined internal audit in Johannesburg eight months ago from the payroll team she supervised. Her supervisor wants her on a payroll assurance engagement because she knows the system best. Before planning starts, Lindiwe discloses her former role and offers to work on another engagement.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Objectivity is personal. Never assess what you once ran; for assurance, presume impairment within 12 months. Disclose up the line, let the CAE decide the remedy, and use information gained at work for the work only.

exam_traps.trap: Once 12 months have passed, the former responsibility no longer matters.
exam_traps.why: Only the presumption for assurance is tied to 12 months. The rule against assessing an activity you were responsible for has no end date, so 12 months is not a release.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, audit management decides every conflict, the CAE's own included.
exam_traps.why: An impairment of the CAE's own objectivity, real or apparent, is disclosed to the board (Standard 2.3).

key_terms.definition: Each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind when judging evidence.
For assurance, objectivity is presumed impaired when the internal auditor was responsible for the activity in the previous 12 months.
An internal auditor must not assess a specific activity they were previously responsible for; the Standards set no end date.

subtopics.memory_aid: Ran it? Don't rate it. Learned it at work? Use it for the work.

subtopics.name: Roles Beyond Internal Auditing
subtopics.definition: A role beyond internal auditing is a duty, such as compliance, that the chief audit executive holds outside internal audit work; the Standards allow it with safeguards.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Small or fast-changing organizations sometimes need the chief audit executive in another role. The safeguards decide whether that role is acceptable.
how_it_works: Three Lines Model: the first line owns risk, the second supports and challenges, the third, internal audit, gives independent assurance and advice.
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) discusses any role that may impair independence, and its safeguards, with the board and senior management (Standard 7.1).
Must: an ongoing role is written into the charter, and assurance over that area comes from elsewhere, such as an outside provider (Standard 7.1).
Must: a temporary role needs independent third-party assurance during it and for 12 months after, plus a plan to hand it to management (Standard 7.1).
Must: an assurance engagement over a function the CAE is responsible for is overseen by an independent party outside internal audit (Standard 2.2).

cells: Never, even for a while (CISA notes 2A2.3)
Allowed with safeguards the board knows of

rows.label: Ongoing role
cells: Not covered
Written into the charter; assurance obtained another way

rows.label: Temporary role

subtopics.example: A small Lisbon hospital group asks chief audit executive Ines to lead compliance for a year while a new law beds in. Ines discusses the impairment and safeguards with the board and senior management, hires an outside firm for assurance during the year and twelve months after, and sets a handover plan.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Other roles are not banned; they are safeguarded. Discuss them with the board and senior management, write ongoing roles into the charter, get outside assurance, and hand temporary roles back on a plan.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, internal audit refuses any compliance or risk management role, even briefly.
exam_traps.why: Standard 7.1 allows such roles when the board acknowledges the impairment and safeguards are in place.

exam_traps.trap: Outside assurance over a temporary role stops when the role ends.
exam_traps.why: Standard 7.1 requires independent third-party assurance during the temporary role and for the following 12 months.

key_terms.definition: A responsibility the chief audit executive holds beyond internal auditing, such as compliance or risk management.
A competent, objective provider outside both internal audit and the area concerned that gives assurance and reports to the board.
The IIA's model of who owns risk, who supports and challenges, and who gives independent assurance.

subtopics.memory_aid: Other hats need written safeguards and someone else's assurance.

subtopics.name: The Quality Program and Who May Assess
subtopics.definition: The quality assurance and improvement program is the chief audit executive's set of internal and external assessments covering the whole function's conformance and performance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board relies on the quality program to trust the function's work, so it approves the external plan and hears the results itself.
how_it_works: Must: internal assessments combine ongoing monitoring with periodic self-assessments; results go to the board and senior management at least yearly (Standards 12.1, 8.3).
Must: an external assessment at least once in five years, by a qualified and independent assessor or team, or a validated self-assessment (Standard 8.4).
Must: at least one person on the assessing side holds an active Certified Internal Auditor designation (Standard 8.4).
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) discusses the external assessment plan with the board; essential condition: the board approves it and gets the full results (Standard 8.4).
Should: treat another department, a related organization, or two organizations reviewing each other as not independent (Standard 8.4).

rows.label: Parts
cells: Supervision, periodic internal reviews, an outside review (CISA notes 1B6.1 to CISA notes 1B6.3)
The same parts, as one program covering the whole function

rows.label: External assessor
cells: Qualified, independent of the organization, one active CIA (CISA notes 1B6.3)
The same, plus a plan the board approves

rows.label: Results go to
cells: The audit committee
The board and senior management; external results straight from the assessor to the board

subtopics.example: Chief audit executive Kenji in Osaka proposes a self-assessment with independent validation for next year. He brings the plan, the validator's credentials and independence checks to the board, which approves it, and arranges for the validator to present the full results to the board in person.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Quality is a program, not an event: ongoing monitoring, periodic self-assessment and an outside look at least every five years. The CAE plans and reports; the board approves the external plan and hears the results first-hand.

exam_traps.trap: A thorough review by the group's internal control department meets the external assessment requirement.
exam_traps.why: People from another department of the same organization are not independent for this purpose (Standard 8.4). An external assessment needs an assessor independent of the organization.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, the CAE reports the external assessment's results to the board.
exam_traps.why: Under Standard 8.4's essential conditions, the board receives the complete results directly from the assessor.

key_terms.definition: The CAE's program of internal and external assessments covering conformance, performance objectives and continuous improvement.
An independent, qualified outside review of the whole function, required at least once every five years.
A full internal assessment that a qualified, independent outside assessor then validates; it can meet the external requirement.

subtopics.memory_aid: Five years, independent, one active CIA; the board approves the plan and sees the results.

subtopics.name: Nonconformance and Performance Measures
subtopics.definition: Nonconformance is a requirement of the Standards that was not met; performance measures show how well the function meets objectives the board approves.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A hidden gap misleads the board about the assurance it gets. Measures show whether the function delivers what the board expects.
how_it_works: Must: when a requirement cannot be met, document and communicate the circumstance, the alternative actions, their impact and the reason (Standard 4.1).
Must: function-wide nonconformance goes to the board and senior management with its impact (Standard 12.1); an engagement's goes in its final communication (Standard 15.1).
Must: if a law blocks part of the Standards, the rest still applies and the conflict is disclosed (Standard 4.1).
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) sets performance objectives with board and senior management input, measures progress, seeks feedback and plans improvements (Standard 12.2).
Essential condition: the board approves the performance objectives at least yearly (Standard 8.3).
Should: avoid measuring auditors by how many findings they raise or by the reviewed managers' approval (Standard 2.2).

The board and senior management, or readers of the final communication

Objectives the board approves yearly, with targets and action plans

subtopics.example: At a Santiago bank, chief audit executive Valentina learns that a new secrecy law bars her team from reading certain customer files that one standard expects them to examine. She documents the conflict, the alternative procedures, their impact and the reason, discloses it to the board and senior management, and applies every other standard in full.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A missed requirement is disclosed, never hidden: circumstance, alternatives, impact and reason, sent to the people its reach affects. Measure the function against objectives the board approves, and meet shortfalls with action plans.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, a standard can never be missed, so there is never a nonconformance to disclose.
exam_traps.why: The Standards plan for it: the CAE documents and communicates the circumstance, alternative actions, impact and reason (Standard 4.1).

exam_traps.trap: The number of findings each auditor raises is a sound performance measure.
exam_traps.why: It rewards finding things over judging them. Standard 2.2's considerations warn against it; balanced measures cover coverage, quality and stakeholder value.

key_terms.definition: A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.
Meeting the requirements of the Global Internal Audit Standards.

subtopics.memory_aid: Cannot conform? Say what, why, the impact and what you did instead.

topics.topic_name: Running the function and its plan, coming from CISA
topics.overview: Section B is the chief audit executive's desk, which CISA study visits only briefly: methodologies, budget, people and technology, the internal audit strategy, the risk-based plan and coordination with other assurance providers.
can_do: Describe what the chief audit executive reports when resources fall short
Tell what the board approves from what it only reviews
List the matters the plan must flag to the board and senior management
Explain when internal audit may rely on another provider's work

subtopics.name: Running the Function
subtopics.definition: Running the function is the chief audit executive's management work: methodologies, budget, people, technology and outside providers, all serving the strategy and the plan.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without enough money, people and technology the plan cannot be delivered. The duty is to obtain resources and report any shortfall, never to absorb it quietly.
how_it_works: Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) sets, evaluates and updates the function's methodologies and trains internal auditors on them (Standard 9.3).
Must: the CAE builds a budget for the strategy and the plan and seeks the board's approval of it (Standard 10.1).
Must: the CAE tells the board and senior management the impact when money or technology falls short (Standards 10.1, 10.3).
Must: new audit technology comes with auditor training and work with the IT and information security functions (Standard 10.3).
Must: outside providers follow the Standards; the CAE supervises their work and keeps responsibility for it (Standard 12.3).
Syllabus only: job design, rewards and coaching have no Standard behind them; learn them as common usage.

rows.label: Skill gap
cells: Training, an expert or co-sourcing (CISA notes 1B1.4)
The same options, inside the CAE's resource strategy

rows.label: Budget
cells: Reviewed by the audit committee (CISA notes 1A1.4)
Built by the CAE, approved by the board

rows.label: Method
cells: ISACA's framework and published audit programs, tailored (CISA notes 1B1.2)
The function's own methodologies, kept current

rows.label: An outside firm's work
cells: Delegate the work, not the responsibility (CISA notes 1A1.7)
The same: the CAE supervises it and answers for it

subtopics.example: Chief audit executive Oluwaseun in Lagos plans to roll out a data analytics platform. Before launch she budgets for training, agrees access rules with the information security team, and updates the methodology for scripts and evidence. When the board trims the tools budget, she reports the coverage the cut will cost.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The CAE manages resources and answers for them: current methodologies, a board-approved budget, trained people, technology rolled out with IT and security, and supervised outside providers. Shortfalls are reported promptly, never absorbed quietly.

exam_traps.trap: When money runs short, the CAE quietly drops low-risk engagements to stay within budget.
exam_traps.why: Re-ranking by risk is sound, but Standard 10.1 requires the CAE to tell the board and senior management the impact promptly.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, a professional body's published audit programs can serve as the function's method.
exam_traps.why: The CAE must set the function's own methodologies, evaluate and update them, and train auditors on them (Standard 9.3). Outside material may inform them.

key_terms.definition: The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
The plan for the people, money and technology the audit plan needs.
An outside firm or specialist supplying skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.

subtopics.memory_aid: Plan it, fund it, staff it, equip it, and say so when it falls short.

subtopics.name: Strategy and Reporting to the Board
subtopics.definition: The internal audit strategy is the function's plan of action for the next few years; board reporting covers what the Standards require, on the board's terms.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The strategy keeps the function aimed at the organization's needs over several years; steady reporting gives the board what oversight needs.
how_it_works: Must: the strategy holds a vision, strategic objectives and supporting initiatives, reviewed periodically with the board and senior management; board approval is not required (Standard 9.2).
Should: review it sooner when strategy, laws, leaders or quality results change (Standard 9.2).
Must: report the plan and budget, charter or mandate changes, possible impairments, results and quality results to the board and senior management (Standard 8.1).
Essential condition: the board sets, with the chief audit executive (CAE), how often it hears from the CAE and what is escalated to it, and how (Standard 8.1).
Should: meet the board privately at least yearly, and tell senior management such sessions took place unless inappropriate (Standard 6.3).
Common usage: a mission statement says why the function exists; the Standards require only a vision.

columns: In CISA study: strategy and reporting
On the CIA exam: strategy and reporting

rows.label: Strategy
cells: The organization's IT strategy (CISA notes 2A2.4)
Internal audit's own strategy, reviewed with the board and senior management

rows.label: Audience
cells: The audit committee (CISA notes 1A1.4, CISA notes 1B5.3)
The board and senior management, each for its own job

rows.label: Board contact
cells: Urgent findings to the committee chair between meetings (CISA notes 1A1.4)
Required reports, private sessions, escalation on terms the board sets

subtopics.example: Chief audit executive Ahmed at a Cairo telecom reviews his three-year strategy early because the company has just merged with a rival. He updates the vision and initiatives and takes the board and senior management through the changes, recording their input. No board vote is needed.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The strategy is reviewed, not approved. The board and senior management hear the required reports; the board sets with the CAE what is escalated and how, and meets the CAE privately.

exam_traps.trap: As with an IT strategy in CISA study, the internal audit strategy needs the board's approval.
exam_traps.why: Standard 9.2 asks the CAE to review the strategy periodically with the board and senior management. Review is the must; board approval is not required.

key_terms.definition: The function's long-term plan of action: a vision, the objectives that reach it and the initiatives that deliver them.
The desired future state of the internal audit function, often three to five years ahead, that gives the strategy direction.
A meeting of the board and the chief audit executive with no senior management in the room.

subtopics.memory_aid: Strategy: review, not approval. The board: hears the must-reports, on its own terms.

subtopics.name: The Plan: Board-Approved and Dynamic
subtopics.definition: The internal audit plan lists the engagements chosen by risk for a period; it rests on a documented risk assessment, stays dynamic, and the board approves it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The plan decides where assurance goes. The details that cost marks are what must be reported, to whom, and the audit universe's status.
how_it_works: Must: base the plan on a documented risk assessment, at least yearly, with input from the board and senior management (Standard 9.4).
Must: consider coverage of IT governance, fraud risk, compliance and ethics programs, and other high risks (Standard 9.4).
Must: discuss the plan and significant changes with the board and senior management; the board approves both (Standard 9.4).
Must: tell both in time about resource limits, an uncovered high-risk area, conflicting demands, and limits on scope or access (Standard 9.4).
May: an audit universe is one planning approach, not a requirement (Standard 9.4); the syllabus still asks about it.
Should: tell the board of an urgent change at once; formal approval follows soon after (Standard 9.4).

cells: A complete audit universe first (CISA notes 1A3.1)
A documented risk assessment; the universe is optional

rows.label: Approver
cells: The audit committee
The board: the plan and each significant change

Discuss with both; the board approves; urgent changes told at once

Four matters, to the board and senior management together

subtopics.example: Midyear, a Gdansk port's operations director asks chief audit executive Agnieszka to swap a planned cybersecurity assurance engagement for advice on a new berth-booking system. Agnieszka weighs the lost assurance, discusses the conflicting demand with the board and senior management, and asks the board to approve the change.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A risk-based plan rests on a documented yearly assessment, not a complete universe. The board approves the plan and each significant change; both bodies hear, in time, what the plan cannot cover.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, a complete audit universe must exist before the plan can be risk-based.
exam_traps.why: The Standards require a documented risk assessment; an audit universe is one approach named in the considerations. It is useful, not mandatory.

exam_traps.trap: Conflicting demands go to the board first, then to senior management.
exam_traps.why: Standard 9.4 sends the four matters to the board and senior management together and ranks none of them. An invented order is the trap.

key_terms.definition: The list of engagements internal audit intends to carry out in a period, chosen by risk.
Internal audit's list of the units, processes and systems that could be audited.
Competing requests for internal audit services from major stakeholders, such as swapping planned assurance for advice.

subtopics.memory_aid: Assess yearly, keep it moving, board approves, tell both what is missing.

subtopics.name: Coordination and Reliance
subtopics.definition: Coordination is sharing coverage with other assurance providers; reliance is using their work in place of internal audit's own, after judging it trustworthy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Coordination closes gaps and cuts repeated reviews, but reliance without evaluation lends internal audit's name to work it never checked.
how_it_works: Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) coordinates with internal and external assurance providers and considers relying on their work (Standard 9.5).
Must: document the basis for reliance; internal audit's conclusions stay internal audit's responsibility (Standard 9.5).
Should: judge each provider's independence, competency, objectivity and due care, and understand its objectives, scope and results, before relying (Standard 9.5).
May: an assurance map shows which provider covers each significant risk; it is a tool, not a requirement (Standard 9.5).
Must: when coordination fails, raise the concern with senior management first, and with the board if needed (Standard 9.5).

columns: On the CIA exam: other providers

rows.label: Before relying
cells: Check competence and objectivity, then the work (CISA notes 1A1.7)
The same, plus a documented basis for reliance

rows.label: Responsibility
cells: Delegate the work, not the responsibility
The same: the conclusions stay internal audit's

rows.label: Coordination
cells: Avoid duplicated work with the external auditor (CISA notes 1A1.4)
A must, across all providers; problems go to senior management, then the board

subtopics.example: At a Vancouver mining company, the second-line safety team has tested site inspection controls all year. Chief audit executive Sophie reviews the team's methods, its objectivity toward site managers and its workpapers, reperforms a few tests, documents why most of the work can be relied on, and plans fresh testing only where gaps remain.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Coordinate to close gaps and cut duplication; rely only after evaluating, with the basis documented. Whatever is relied on, the conclusions remain internal audit's, and coordination problems go to senior management first.

exam_traps.trap: A respected outside firm's report can be relied on as delivered.
exam_traps.why: Reputation is not evidence. The CAE evaluates the provider and its work, documents the basis for reliance and stays responsible for the conclusions.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, a coordination problem goes straight to the audit committee.
exam_traps.why: Standard 9.5 has the CAE raise it with senior management first, and with the board if necessary.

key_terms.definition: Any internal or external party that gives assurance, such as compliance, risk management or the external auditor.
Using another party's work or information instead of repeating it, after judging it trustworthy.
A table of significant risks and who gives assurance over each.

subtopics.memory_aid: Coordinate, evaluate, document, and keep the conclusion your own.

topics.overview: Section C reuses most CISA planning skill. The changes are who approves objectives and scope, where criteria come from, planning without the audit risk model, recognize-level business knowledge, Topical Requirements and advisory exceptions.
can_do: Route a scope limitation from discovery to the board
Choose criteria in the order the Standards set
Plan an engagement risk assessment without the audit risk model
Tell when a Topical Requirement applies

subtopics.name: Objectives, Scope and Who Approves
subtopics.definition: Engagement objectives say what an engagement will determine; scope says what it covers. The chief audit executive, or a delegated supervisor, approves both and any change.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Objectives and scope decide what assurance an engagement can give. Unapproved changes or unreported limits leave readers trusting more than the work supports.
how_it_works: Must: objectives and scope, and any change to them, are approved by the chief audit executive (CAE) or a supervisor the CAE delegates to (Standard 13.3).
Must: tell management the objectives, scope and timing, and any later change, in time (Standard 13.1).
Must: discuss a scope limitation with management to resolve it; if it stays unresolved, the CAE takes it to the board (Standard 13.3).
Must: an assurance final communication explains any scope limitation (Standard 15.1).
Should: in assurance work internal auditors mainly set objectives and scope; in advisory work they typically set them with management (Standard 13.3).
Must: the CAE, or a delegate, approves the work program before use and promptly after any change (Standard 13.6).

rows.label: Program change
cells: Updated 'with approval' (CISA notes 1B1.2)
Approved promptly by the CAE or a delegated supervisor

rows.label: Scope limitation
cells: Dealt with through the opinion at reporting (CISA notes 1B5.4)
Discussed when found; if unresolved, the CAE takes it to the board

subtopics.example: Halfway through a contracts engagement at a Kuala Lumpur builder, auditor Farah finds that a joint-venture partner holds the records she needs and will not release them. She asks the project director to obtain them, documents the refusal, and tells her supervisor, who briefs chief audit executive Raj. Farah notes the limitation for the final communication.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Scope follows risk; its approvals follow the seat. The CAE, or a delegated supervisor, approves objectives, scope, the work program and changes. A scope limitation is discussed first, taken to the board by the CAE if unresolved, and explained.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, a scope limitation is dealt with at the end, through the overall verdict.
exam_traps.why: The Standards act when it is found: discuss it with management to resolve it, and if that fails the CAE takes it to the board. The final communication then explains it.

exam_traps.trap: The engagement auditor may widen the scope mid-fieldwork when a new risk is obvious.
exam_traps.why: A change to objectives or scope needs approval by the CAE or a delegated supervisor first, and management is then told in time.

key_terms.definition: What an engagement will and will not cover.
A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.

subtopics.memory_aid: Hit a wall? Talk to management, tell the line, let the CAE take it up.

subtopics.name: Criteria: Management's First
subtopics.definition: Evaluation criteria are the yardstick an engagement measures against; internal auditors first judge whether the criteria the board and senior management set are adequate.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Criteria the organization already accepts make findings hard to dispute. Criteria nobody agreed invite an argument about the yardstick instead of the gap.
how_it_works: Must: identify the criteria most relevant to the engagement's objectives and scope (Standard 13.4).
Must: judge whether the board and senior management have set adequate criteria; if they have, use them (Standard 13.4).
Must: if they are inadequate, find appropriate criteria through discussion with the board, senior management or both (Standard 13.4).
May: frameworks, laws, contracts and industry standards can serve as criteria when they are adequate (Standard 13.4).
May: advisory work may need no criteria, depending on the agreement with stakeholders (Standard 13.4).
Should: tell management which criteria will be used, and document the agreement (Standard 13.4).

rows.label: First source
cells: Policy, standard, regulation or contract (CISA notes 1B5.1)
Adequate criteria the board and senior management have set

rows.label: Policy is silent
cells: A recognized framework, agreed as criteria (the CISA bank's 'No Internal Policy Applies' items)
Appropriate criteria found through discussion with the board, senior management or both

rows.label: Advisory work
cells: Not covered
Criteria may not be needed

subtopics.example: At a Brisbane council, auditor Liam plans an engagement on fleet fuel cards. The council's policy sets spending limits but says nothing on how often card use is reviewed. Liam uses the limits, which are adequate, agrees a review-frequency criterion with the chief financial officer before testing, and tells the fleet manager which criteria apply.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Criteria start at home: use the board's and senior management's criteria when they are adequate, and settle better ones with senior management, the board or both when they are not. A framework can serve as criteria; it never skips that first judgment.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, where policy is silent, a recognized IT control framework becomes the criteria.
exam_traps.why: First judge what the board and senior management have set, then find appropriate criteria through discussion with them (Standard 13.4). A framework may be the result, never the shortcut.

exam_traps.trap: Internal auditors may replace management's adequate criteria with better ones from good practice.
exam_traps.why: Adequate criteria must be used. Auditors may suggest better ones, but suggesting is not replacing.

key_terms.definition: The yardstick for an engagement: what the activity should look like, taken from policy, law, contracts or good practice.
Criteria that fit the engagement's subject, match what the organization and the activity aim for, and allow a reliable comparison.

subtopics.memory_aid: Theirs first, if adequate; agreed with the top, if not.

subtopics.name: Risk Assessment Without the Audit Risk Model
subtopics.definition: The engagement risk assessment finds and ranks the significant risks to the activity's objectives, fraud included; the Standards use no audit risk formula.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The risk assessment decides where the engagement spends its time. Planning from the activity's own objectives keeps the work on what matters to the organization.
how_it_works: Must: understand the activity, identify the significant risks to its objectives, and prioritize them (Standard 13.2).
Must: consider specific fraud risks in every engagement risk assessment; advisory work may not need a formal, documented one (Standard 13.2).
Must: judge significance by likelihood and impact. 'Significance' is the defined term; 'materiality' appears a few times without a threshold model (Standard 14.3).
The glossary defines inherent risk and residual risk; it has no control risk, detection risk or audit risk.
Syllabus line: the fraud triangle's three conditions are motivation (pressure), opportunity and rationalization; the Standards say nothing more on it.

columns: On the CIA exam: planning risk

rows.label: Model
cells: Audit risk = inherent x control x detection (CISA notes 1A3.5)
No model; the engagement risk assessment

rows.label: Threshold
cells: Materiality as a planning threshold (CISA notes 1A3.6)
Significance: likelihood and impact

rows.label: Test mix
cells: Compliance, then substantive testing (CISA notes 1B2.1)
Procedures on control design, effectiveness and efficiency

rows.label: Fraud
cells: Handled when red flags appear (CISA notes 1B3.5)
Considered in every engagement risk assessment

subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on a Bogota hospital's pharmacy stock, auditor Camila lists the pharmacy's objectives and ranks its risks by likelihood and impact. She adds a fraud risk, theft of controlled drugs on night shifts, because access is wide and counts are self-reported. The list shapes the objectives she proposes.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan from the activity's objectives and risks, not from a formula. Rank by likelihood and impact, consider fraud in every engagement risk assessment, and use 'significance', not detection risk, to say how much a matter counts.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, the auditor lowers audit risk by setting detection risk and adding substantive tests.
exam_traps.why: The Standards have no audit risk model. An option built on detection risk is written in another body's lens; the CIA answer works from the engagement risk assessment.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud risk is considered only after red flags appear in fieldwork.
exam_traps.why: Standard 13.2 requires specific fraud risks to be considered in every engagement risk assessment, at planning.

key_terms.definition: The planning step that identifies and ranks the risks of the activity being examined.
The exposure an activity carries before counting anything management does about it.
How much a matter counts in its setting, weighing size as well as nature.
A model of three conditions that accompany fraud: motivation (incentive or pressure), opportunity (a gap in control) and rationalization (the excuse).

subtopics.memory_aid: No formula: objectives, risks, fraud, likelihood and impact.

subtopics.name: A Scope Wider Than IT
subtopics.definition: Section C asks you to recognize IT, finance and business-process risks when planning, and to fit the approach and resources to the engagement; relevance matters more than depth.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Planning questions ask what a fact means for the engagement: a risk to assess, a procedure to plan, a resource to find. Deep technical detail rarely decides them.
how_it_works: Syllabus line: recognize cyber risks, IT general controls, why IT control frameworks are used, data privacy, and continuity and recovery readiness; recognize, not configure.
Syllabus line: recognize finance and accounting terms, such as assets, liabilities and capital, and the risks in processes such as purchasing, inventory and payables.
Syllabus line: choose among traditional, agile, integrated and remote approaches; the Standards rank none, so fit to the objectives decides.
Must: identify the resources the engagement needs; if they are not enough, internal auditors discuss it with the chief audit executive (Standard 13.5).
Must: every approach keeps the evidence, supervision and documentation rules; agile changes timing, and remote work changes location (Standards 14.1, 12.3, 14.6).

Recognize the risk and the kind of control

rows.label: Finance and processes

rows.label: Approach
cells: Agile and integrated audits (CISA notes 1B1.5, CISA notes 1A2.4)
The same names, plus remote; chosen by fit

subtopics.example: Arjun, auditing purchasing at a Pune manufacturer, finds that buyers can create new suppliers in the purchasing system. Rather than drafting a configuration fix, he notes the risk of payments to fictitious suppliers, adds a supplier-master test to the work program for his supervisor's approval, and asks finance for a year of supplier payments.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize the risk, name the kind of control, and ask what it means for the engagement's objectives, scope and resources. The internal auditor plans and tests; management designs and fixes. Fit the approach to the objectives without lowering a must.

exam_traps.trap: Answering as the IT specialist: the best planning answer is the most detailed technical control fix.
exam_traps.why: Planning questions ask what the fact means for the engagement: a risk to assess, a procedure to plan, a resource to obtain. Designing the fix is management's job.

exam_traps.trap: An agile engagement may lighten documentation because results come sooner.
exam_traps.why: The approach changes timing and delivery, not the requirements. Evidence, supervision and documentation rules apply in every cycle.

key_terms.definition: Common usage: controls over the whole IT environment, such as access, change and operations, that every system relies on.
A new or fast-changing risk with little history, whose likelihood and impact are still uncertain.

subtopics.memory_aid: Recognize, relate, plan; the fix belongs to management.

subtopics.name: Topical Requirements and Advisory Work
subtopics.definition: A Topical Requirement is a mandatory baseline for engagements on a named subject; advisory work follows the Standards too, except where a standard relaxes a step.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Both change which steps an engagement must take, so both belong in planning, before the work starts.
how_it_works: Must: when an engagement's scope includes the topic, assurance work conforms with the Topical Requirement; for advisory work, conformance is recommended.
Must: assess each requirement for applicability and document every exclusion with its reason (Cybersecurity Topical Requirement).
It applies when a planned engagement covers the topic, the topic arises during an engagement, or an unplanned engagement on it is requested.
Exam dates: Cybersecurity is testable now; The IIA's list starts Third-Party in March, Organizational Behavior in June and Organizational Resilience in October 2027.
May: advisory work may leave out a formal risk assessment, criteria and evidence-based findings when the agreement allows (Standards 13.2, 13.4, 14.2).
Must: advisory work on an area you were responsible for needs disclosure to the requesting party before you accept (Standard 2.2).

Topical Requirements, mandatory for assurance in scope

rows.label: Advisory work
cells: Allowed with agreed terms and safeguards (CISA notes 1A2.2)
The same Standards, with stated exceptions

subtopics.example: During an assurance engagement on claims at a Warsaw insurer, auditor Tomasz finds the claims system's cyber controls inside the scope. His supervisor has him assess each part of the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement for applicability, and he documents why two parts do not apply.
subtopics.isaca_rule: A Topical Requirement binds assurance work whose scope includes its topic: assess each requirement and document exclusions. Advisory work follows the Standards except where one relaxes a step.

exam_traps.why: It also applies when the topic arises during an engagement or an unplanned engagement on it is requested.

exam_traps.trap: A habit from assurance work: every advisory engagement needs formal criteria and evidence-based findings.
exam_traps.why: The Standards apply to advisory work, but a formal risk assessment, criteria and evidence-based findings may be left out when the agreement allows (Standards 13.2, 13.4, 14.2).

key_terms.definition: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.

topics.overview: Section D, the largest section, is the most familiar ground. Watch three shifts: The IIA's three evidence qualities, an engagement conclusion in place of an opinion, and a way up that runs through the chief audit executive.
