Turn findings into an engagement conclusion without opinion types
Name who reviews and who approves engagement documentation

subtopics.name: Relevant, Reliable, Sufficient
subtopics.definition: Relevant, reliable and sufficient are the three qualities Standard 14.1 requires of the information behind engagement results; 'appropriate' is not one of them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Results are only as good as the information behind them. The three qualities, and what makes information reliable, decide many Section D questions.
how_it_works: Must: information is relevant, reliable and sufficient; evaluate all three, and gather more when it falls short (Standard 14.1).
Must: reliability rises when the auditor obtains it first-hand or from an independent source, when it is corroborated, and when its source system is well controlled (Standard 14.1).
Must: sufficient means a prudent, informed, competent person could repeat the work and reach the same conclusions (Standard 14.1).
Must: when relevant evidence cannot be obtained, decide whether that is itself a finding (Standard 14.1).
The IIA's documents list the three words in different orders; learn the qualities, not a sequence.
Walk-throughs, interviews, observation and questionnaires gather information; statements describe a process, while records and data show how it ran.

columns: On the CIA exam: evidence words

rows.label: Named qualities
cells: Sufficient and appropriate, where appropriate means relevant and reliable (CISA notes 1B3.1)
Relevant, reliable, sufficient

rows.label: Reliability
cells: A long ranking, such as originals over copies (CISA notes 1B3.2)
Three factors: who obtained it, corroboration, the source system's controls

rows.label: Evidence not obtainable
cells: A scope limitation for the opinion (CISA notes 1B5.4)
Decide whether it is itself a finding

rows.label: Walk-through
cells: Traces one transaction end to end (CISA notes 1A3.4)
The same common meaning; the Standards do not define it

subtopics.example: Testing refunds at a Casablanca retailer, auditor Youssef receives a spreadsheet of approvals prepared by the refunds supervisor. He runs his own extract from the point-of-sale system, matches it to the approvals, and finds forty refunds missing from the spreadsheet. He records the gap and uses the system data, not the supervisor's file, as his evidence.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Three qualities, three questions: does it address the objective, can it be trusted, is there enough for a competent stranger to agree? Reliability rises with first-hand or independent sourcing, corroboration and a well-controlled source. Missing evidence may itself be a finding.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, evidence that is sufficient and appropriate meets the Standards.
exam_traps.why: The Standards name three qualities: relevant, reliable and sufficient. An option using 'appropriate' signals another body's vocabulary; test it against the three.

exam_traps.trap: More of the same evidence fixes a reliability problem.
exam_traps.why: Volume answers sufficiency only. Reliability needs a better source: first-hand, independent, corroborated, or from a system with effective controls.

key_terms.definition: Confirming information against a second, separate source.
Following one transaction from start to finish to see how the process really works.
An unbiased, questioning attitude: critically assessing whether information is reliable before relying on it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Relevant, reliable, sufficient: on point, trustworthy, enough for a stranger.

subtopics.name: Tools and Analytics at Syllabus Depth
subtopics.definition: Section D's technology and analytics topics ask you to recognize tools, data types, analytics steps and analytical reviews, and to choose the one that fits.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These topics test judgment about fit: which technique answers the objective and what its result means, not how a tool is configured.
how_it_works: Syllabus line: know what tools such as dashboards, bots, embedded audit modules and continuous monitoring do, and the data each needs.
Syllabus line: analytics runs from the question to the data, its cleanup, the analysis and the report; analysis can be diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive, anomaly detection or text analysis.
Syllabus line: ratios, trends, variances and benchmarking show where to look; follow-up against criteria turns a difference into a potential finding.
Must: use tools and techniques that fit the work, as part of due professional care (Standard 4.2).
Should: sample representatively, or test the whole population with software, and record the approach (Standard 14.1).

columns: On the CIA exam: audit technology

rows.label: Depth
cells: Named online techniques and sampling terms (CISA notes 1B4.3, CISA notes 1B2.3)
Recognize the tool and the result it gives

rows.label: Sampling
cells: Statistical plans, confidence and precision (CISA notes 1B2.2 to CISA notes 1B2.6)
A representative sample or the whole population, a should

subtopics.example: Auditor Mei, reviewing credit notes at a Taipei distributor, runs anomaly detection across a full year of transactions. Twelve credit notes, all approved by one manager just after quarter end, stand out. Mei treats them as leads, pulls the supporting documents, and compares each with the credit policy before calling any of them a finding.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Pick the technique whose answer is the objective's answer. Tools and analytics show where to look; only follow-up against criteria turns a pattern into a potential finding, and the judgment stays with the internal auditor.

exam_traps.trap: An anomaly flagged by analytics is a finding.
exam_traps.why: A flag is a lead. It becomes a potential finding only after follow-up shows a gap between the condition and the criteria (Standard 14.2).

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, a sampling answer turns on confidence level and precision.
exam_traps.why: The Standards mention sampling only in considerations, asking for a representative sample or a whole-population test; the syllabus names no sampling formula.

key_terms.definition: Using software to examine whole sets of data for patterns, trends and exceptions.
A diagram of a process's steps, people and decision points, from start to finish.
Analysis that picks out items that stand apart from the usual pattern, as leads to follow up.

subtopics.memory_aid: Tools find leads; criteria make findings.

subtopics.name: From Finding to Engagement Conclusion
subtopics.definition: A finding is the gap between criteria and condition; the engagement conclusion is the internal auditors' overall judgment on the findings taken together.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The conclusion is what readers act on. It says plainly how effective governance, risk management and control are, even when everything works.
how_it_works: Must: compare the condition with the criteria; each difference is a potential finding to evaluate (Standard 14.2).
Must: identify root causes, with management when possible, and the potential effects (Standard 14.3).
Must: judge significance by likelihood and impact; report a significant risk as a finding; rank findings by the chief audit executive's method (Standard 14.3).
Must: the conclusion weighs the findings' overall significance; for assurance it says how effective governance, risk management and control are (Standard 14.5).
Must: when no gap is found and the work is enough, say that the processes are effective (Standard 14.2).
May: express the conclusion on a rating scale, for consistency (Standard 14.5).

columns: On the CIA exam: the verdict

rows.label: Parts of a finding
cells: Criteria, condition, cause, effect, recommendation (CISA notes 1B5.1)
The same parts; root cause with management when possible

rows.label: Weight
cells: Materiality and a severity rating (CISA notes 1A3.6, CISA notes 1B5.1)
Significance, ranked by the chief audit executive's method

rows.label: Overall verdict
cells: Unmodified, qualified, adverse or disclaimer (CISA notes 1B5.4)
An engagement conclusion on effectiveness; no opinion types

subtopics.example: Auditor Bilal closes an engagement on branch cash at a Karachi bank. Three findings share one cause: vault counts are signed by the teller who keeps the keys. He weighs them together as one significant weakness and drafts a conclusion that cash controls are not effective.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Gap first, then cause, effect and significance; then weigh the findings together. The verdict is an engagement conclusion on how effective governance, risk management and control are, stated plainly whether the news is good or bad.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, two significant but contained weaknesses call for a qualified opinion.
exam_traps.why: The Standards have no opinion types. The internal auditor states an engagement conclusion on effectiveness, judging the findings' combined significance.

exam_traps.trap: With no findings, the final communication can leave out a conclusion.
exam_traps.why: When no gap is found and the work is sufficient, Standard 14.2 asks the internal auditor to give assurance that the processes are effective.

key_terms.definition: A gap between what the internal auditors found (the condition) and what should be there (the criteria).
What the internal auditors actually found: the existing state of the activity.
The auditors' overall verdict on the engagement results, taken together.
A defined set of levels the function uses to express an overall assessment consistently.

subtopics.memory_aid: Gap, cause, weight, together: one conclusion on effectiveness.

subtopics.name: Workpapers, Supervision and Speaking Up
subtopics.definition: Workpapers are the engagement's documented record; supervision checks the work from planning to sign-off; speaking up means raising problems through the supervisor to the chief audit executive.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The file is the proof behind every result, and the route upward decides who can act on a problem. Both have fixed owners.
how_it_works: Must: document so an informed, prudent, competent person could repeat the work and reach the same results (Standard 14.6).
Must: internal auditors and the engagement supervisor review the documentation; the chief audit executive (CAE), or a delegate, approves it (Standard 14.6).
Must: keep records as law, regulation and policy require (Standard 14.6).
Must: supervision runs through the whole engagement and its evidence is kept; the CAE may delegate it, never the accountability (Standard 12.3).
Must: on disagreement, discuss and seek mutual understanding; results change only for a valid reason (Standard 13.1).
Route: scope limitations to management, then the CAE; resource gaps and impairments to the CAE; violations to those able to act (Standards 13.3, 2.3, 1.3).

columns: In CISA study: the file and the route
On the CIA exam: the file and the route

rows.label: Test of the file
cells: An experienced auditor could follow the trail (CISA notes 1B1.3)
A competent stranger could repeat the work and agree

rows.label: Approves the file
cells: Supervisors review it (CISA notes 1B6.1)
The CAE, or a supervisor the CAE delegates to

rows.label: Pressure on findings
cells: Repeated pressure goes to the audit committee (CISA notes 1A1.4, CISA notes 1B5.5)
Through the supervisor to the CAE, who takes matters to the board

subtopics.example: At a Hanoi shipping firm, the logistics director tells auditor Linh to drop a late-delivery finding before the draft goes out. Linh discusses the evidence with him, hears no new facts, keeps the finding and records his view. She then tells her engagement supervisor, who briefs the chief audit executive about the pressure.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Document for a competent stranger, review before results go out, and let the CAE or a delegate approve the file. Problems travel up through the supervisor to the CAE; reaching the board is the CAE's step.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, under pressure to drop a finding, the auditor writes to the audit committee chair.
exam_traps.why: The auditor keeps the finding, records the disagreement and takes the pressure to the supervisor and the CAE. The CAE decides what reaches the board.

key_terms.definition: The engagement's documented record of the planning, tests and evidence behind its results, kept to the function's methodology.
The workpapers and other documents created or collected during an engagement.
Passing a matter to a higher authority because the current level cannot, or should not, settle it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Write for a stranger; route through the CAE.

topics.topic_name: Results and monitoring, coming from CISA
topics.overview: Section E keeps the steps a CISA holder knows, from drafting results to follow-up, and changes who acts at each one. The chief audit executive approves, sends, corrects, judges accepted risk and escalates.
can_do: Name the required parts of a final communication
Choose among recommending, requesting an action plan and agreeing actions
Put the risk acceptance steps in order, each at its strength
Describe what happens when an action plan slips

subtopics.name: The Final Engagement Communication
subtopics.definition: The final engagement communication carries an engagement's results; internal auditors draft it, and the chief audit executive approves it and decides who receives it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The final communication is the record the board and management act on. Its content is fixed, and drafting, approving and sending sit with different seats.
how_it_works: Must: give the objectives, scope, conclusions, any recommendations or action plans, and who acts by when (Standard 15.1).
Must: for assurance, add the findings with their significance and priority, any scope limitation, and a conclusion on effectiveness (Standard 15.1).
Must: acknowledge actions management started or finished before issue; a fixed finding is still reported (Standard 15.1).
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) approves it before issue, decides who receives it, and seeks required advice before an outside release (Standards 15.1, 11.3).
Must: correct a significant error or omission promptly for everyone who got the original, judged by criteria agreed with the board (Standard 11.4).
Must: meet the seven qualities: accurate, objective, clear, concise, constructive, complete, timely (Standards 11.2, 15.1).

columns: On the CIA exam: the report

rows.label: Who issues it
cells: The IS auditor (CISA notes 1B5.3)
Internal auditors draft; the CAE approves and sends it

rows.label: Sent to
cells: The audit committee, with copies to managers who act
Parties who can give the results due consideration, chosen by the CAE

rows.label: Fixed during fieldwork
cells: Still reported, with the fix noted (CISA notes 1B5.1)
The same: the action is acknowledged

rows.label: Conformance wording
cells: Not covered
A should, only when supervision and quality results support it

subtopics.example: Auditor Grace in Kampala drafts the final communication for a grants engagement; chief audit executive Moses approves it. A week after issue, finance shows one finding double-counted two grants. Moses judges the error significant under the board-agreed criteria and sends corrected information to everyone who received the original.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal auditors draft; the CAE approves, chooses recipients and seeks advice before any outside release. Content is fixed, already-fixed findings are acknowledged, not dropped, and a significant error goes back to every original recipient.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, the internal auditor issues the report straight to the audit committee.
exam_traps.why: The CAE reviews and approves the final communication before issue and decides who receives it and how (Standards 15.1, 11.3). The auditor drafts.

exam_traps.trap: Every final communication must say the engagement conformed with the Standards.
exam_traps.why: The statement is a should, fitting only when supervision and quality results support it. The must runs the other way: nonconformance is disclosed.

key_terms.definition: The communication issued at the end of an engagement with its results, often a written report.
A final-communication sentence saying the engagement was conducted in conformance with the Standards; it should appear only when supervision and quality program results support it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Auditors draft; the CAE approves, sends and corrects.

subtopics.name: Recommendations, Action Plans and Disagreement
subtopics.definition: For each finding, internal auditors recommend, ask management for an action plan, or agree actions together; management carries them out, and disagreement follows a set method.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Actions shaped with the people who run the activity are more likely to fix the root cause, and a set method keeps disagreement visible.
how_it_works: Must: decide, finding by finding, whether to recommend, request an action plan or agree actions jointly (Standard 14.4).
Must: discuss recommendations with the management of the activity under review (Standard 14.4); should: discuss action plans' feasibility too. Management implements.
Should: actions address the root cause and bring the risk to an acceptable level, with cost weighed against benefit (Standard 14.4).
Must: on disagreement, discuss, seek mutual understanding, and change results only for a valid reason (Standard 13.1).
Must: follow a set method that lets both sides state their positions on the final communication (Standard 13.1).
May: hold a closing communication (an exit conference) to settle the results with management before issue (Standard 13.1).

columns: On the CIA exam: agreeing actions

rows.label: Routes
cells: The IS auditor recommends; management decides (CISA notes 1B5.1)
Recommend, request an action plan, or agree jointly

rows.label: Closing meeting
cells: The exit meeting, a fixed step (CISA notes 1B5.2)
A closing communication that may be held

rows.label: Disagreement
cells: Kept at the auditor's rating, with management's view beside it (CISA notes 1B5.2)
The same direction, through a set method

subtopics.example: At a Montevideo dairy, auditor Sofia finds that tank temperature alarms are often silenced without a log. She asks the plant manager for an action plan rather than prescribing one, because his engineers know the sensors. At the closing communication they discuss his plan; she judges whether it reaches the cause and records the owner and date.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the route most likely to fix the root cause: recommend, request an action plan, or agree together. Discuss it with the people who run the activity; on disagreement, seek understanding, record both positions, and change results only for a valid reason.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, the exit conference is a fixed step before any final communication.
exam_traps.why: Standard 13.1's considerations say a closing communication may be held, depending on the engagement. Communicating throughout is required; this meeting is not.

exam_traps.trap: A finding is softened when management disagrees strongly.
exam_traps.why: Results change only for a valid reason, such as new evidence. Otherwise both positions are recorded through the function's set method.

key_terms.definition: A discussion before the final communication, also called an exit conference, where auditors and management finalize the results.
An action internal auditors propose to close a gap, reduce a risk or improve the activity under review.

subtopics.memory_aid: Recommend, request or agree; always discuss; change only for a reason.

subtopics.name: Ratings, Themes and Wider Conclusions
subtopics.definition: Prioritizing ranks findings by significance; residual risk is what remains after controls that work; themes and wider conclusions carry results beyond one engagement to the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Ratings that mean the same everywhere let the board compare risks, and patterns across engagements can show causes no single engagement reveals.
how_it_works: Must: rank findings by significance using the chief audit executive's (CAE's) method, so ratings mean the same in every engagement (Standard 14.3).
Syllabus line: judge residual risk after evaluating control design and effectiveness, counting only the controls that work.
May: use a rating scale for the overall assessment, defined in the CAE's methodology (Standard 14.5).
Must: communicate themes across engagements to the board and senior management in time, with insights, advice or conclusions (Standard 11.3).
Must: a conclusion on a business unit or the whole organization states the request, criteria, scope, supporting information and any reliance on other providers (Standard 11.3).

rows.label: Per finding
cells: A severity rating (CISA notes 1B5.1)
Significance by likelihood and impact, ranked by one method

rows.label: Overall
cells: An opinion type (CISA notes 1B5.4)
A conclusion, optionally on a rating scale

rows.label: Across engagements
cells: Recurring findings escalated (CISA notes 1B5.5)
Themes and wider conclusions to the board and senior management

subtopics.example: Reviewing a year of engagements at a Seoul electronics maker, chief audit executive Ji-woo sees moderate access-review findings at five plants. Together they point to one cause: an access policy no one owns. She reports the theme, its cause and her advice to the board and senior management.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank every finding with one method, judge residual risk only after evaluating the controls, and look across engagements. Themes and wider conclusions go to the board and senior management in time, with their basis shown.

exam_traps.trap: Each engagement may use its own rating scale, as long as it is explained.
exam_traps.why: Findings are ranked by significance using the CAE's methodology, so ratings mean the same across engagements (Standard 14.3).

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, only findings that recur in the same area need reporting beyond their own reports.
exam_traps.why: Different findings across engagements can form a theme, which Standard 11.3 requires the CAE to communicate in time to the board and senior management.

key_terms.definition: Patterns or trends across several engagements, such as a shared root cause or a practice worth spreading.
The CAE's judgment on governance, risk management or control for a business unit or the whole organization, drawn from several engagements.
The exposure still left once management's controls and other responses are in place.

subtopics.memory_aid: One scale, residual after controls, look across, tell the board.

subtopics.name: When Management Accepts Too Much Risk
subtopics.definition: Communicating risk acceptance is the chief audit executive's duty when management has accepted risk above the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance; resolving the risk is not.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Risk above the organization's appetite threatens objectives the board answers for. The Standards set a trigger and a sequence, each step at its own strength.
how_it_works: Must: the trigger is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) conclusion that accepted risk goes beyond the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance, not personal comfort (Standard 11.5).
Should: first raise it with the managers who own the risk and try to agree an updated action plan (Standard 11.5).
Must: if it stays unresolved, discuss the matter with senior management (Standard 11.5).
Must: if the CAE judges that senior management has not resolved it, escalate it to the board (Standard 11.5).
Must: resolving the risk is not the CAE's responsibility (Standard 11.5).

columns: On the CIA exam: accepted risk

rows.label: Test
cells: Within risk appetite and properly approved? (CISA notes 1B5.5, CISA notes 2A5.2)
Above the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance?

rows.label: First step
cells: Confirm the approval
Should: the responsible management

rows.label: Then
cells: Report it to the audit committee
Must: senior management; then the board if unresolved

rows.label: Who resolves it
cells: The level the risk policy names (CISA notes 2A5.2)
Management and the board; never the CAE

subtopics.example: At a Tbilisi bank, IT management signs a waiver keeping an unsupported core database two more years, beyond the board's tolerance for unpatched systems. Chief audit executive Nino raises it with the IT director, then with the chief executive and chief risk officer. When they let it stand, she takes it to the board.
subtopics.isaca_rule: The test is the organization's risk appetite or tolerance. Raise it with responsible management (should), discuss with senior management (must), escalate to the board if the CAE judges it unresolved (must). The CAE communicates; management and the board decide.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, once the acceptance is properly approved, report it to the audit committee and stop.
exam_traps.why: An approved acceptance can still exceed risk appetite or tolerance; then the CAE must discuss it with senior management (Standard 11.5).

exam_traps.trap: The CAE is required to raise it with the responsible manager before anyone else.
exam_traps.why: That first step is a should, in the considerations. The requirements begin at senior management, then the board.

key_terms.definition: How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.
A knowing decision to bear a risk without further action.
The managers who own the risk in question and can act on it; the CAE should raise concerns with them first.

subtopics.memory_aid: Owner first (should), senior management (must), board if unresolved (must).

subtopics.name: Confirming Actions and Escalating
subtopics.definition: Confirming implementation means internal audit checks that management carried out its recommendations or action plans; dates that keep slipping can amount to accepting risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A finding helps only when its action is carried out. Tracking shows which risks stay open, and slipping dates can be a decision in disguise.
how_it_works: Must: confirm that management implemented its recommendations or action plans, by a set method; management does the implementing (Standard 15.2).
Must: inquire about progress, do follow-up assessments by risk, and keep a tracking system current; how far each step goes follows significance (Standard 15.2).
KaiSip's reading: test the actions on significant findings; for minor ones, inquiry backed by evidence may do.
Must: when dates slip, get and document management's explanation and take it to the chief audit executive (CAE) (Standard 15.2).
Must: the CAE decides whether the delay means senior management accepted risk beyond tolerance; if so, the risk acceptance sequence follows (Standards 15.2, 11.5).
Must: monitoring results go to the board and senior management (Standard 8.1).

rows.label: Method
cells: Independent verification scaled to risk (CISA notes 1B5.5)
Inquire, assess by risk, track; depth follows significance

rows.label: Late actions
cells: Recurring findings escalated to the audit committee (CISA notes 1B5.5)
Explanation documented; the CAE judges whether risk was accepted

rows.label: Route up
cells: The audit committee
Responsible management (should), senior management, then the board

subtopics.example: Auditor Tariq tracks a Doha retailer's plan to fix gift-card refund controls, now four months late for the second time. He asks the finance manager why, documents the answer, a vendor delay with no interim control, and takes it to chief audit executive Layla.
subtopics.isaca_rule: Confirm, do not implement: inquire, assess by risk and track every action. A slipping date is documented and taken to the CAE, who judges whether it is accepted risk beyond tolerance; if so, Standard 11.5's sequence follows.

exam_traps.trap: Management's written confirmation that an action is complete closes it.
exam_traps.why: A statement is a start. Follow-up assessments by risk test whether the action was implemented; the tracking record closes only when that is confirmed.

exam_traps.trap: As in CISA study, repeatedly overdue actions go straight to the audit committee.
exam_traps.why: The auditor documents management's explanation and takes it to the CAE, who judges whether the delay is accepted risk; the sequence then starts with senior management.

key_terms.definition: A tool, such as a database or spreadsheet, that records each action's owner, due date and status.
Testing done after management reports an action complete, to confirm it was implemented and addresses the finding.

subtopics.memory_aid: Ask, assess, track; slipping dates go to the CAE.

key_terminologies.IS auditor: CIA term: internal auditor. The remit covers all of governance, risk management and control, not only information systems.
key_terminologies.Audit committee: CIA term: board. The Standards' board is the highest governing body, which can be an audit committee.
key_terminologies.Audit charter: CIA term: internal audit charter, which documents the internal audit mandate; the board approves it.
key_terminologies.Auditee, auditee management: CIA term: the management of the activity under review.
key_terminologies.Audit program: CIA term: work program, also called the engagement work program; the chief audit executive or a delegate approves it.
key_terminologies.Audit manager, audit management: CIA terms: engagement supervisor for one engagement; chief audit executive for the whole function.
key_terminologies.Work papers: CIA terms: workpapers and engagement documentation, approved by the chief audit executive or a delegate.
key_terminologies.Annual audit plan: CIA term: internal audit plan, risk-based, dynamic and approved by the board.
key_terminologies.Sufficient and appropriate evidence: CIA terms: relevant, reliable and sufficient information. 'Appropriate' is not one of the Standards' words for it.
key_terminologies.Materiality: CIA term: significance, judged by likelihood and impact. 'Materiality' appears a few times in the Standards but is not the defined term.
key_terminologies.Audit risk, control risk, detection risk: No CIA counterpart: the Standards use an engagement risk assessment and define only inherent risk and residual risk.
key_terminologies.Compliance and substantive testing: CIA terms: procedures that evaluate control design, effectiveness and efficiency.
key_terminologies.CAATs: Computer-assisted audit techniques. CIA terms: technology and data analysis tools used in engagements.
key_terminologies.Audit opinion: CIA term: engagement conclusion, a judgment on the findings' overall significance; the four opinion types have no place in it.
key_terminologies.Audit report: CIA term: final engagement communication. The Challenge syllabus also says audit report.
key_terminologies.Exit meeting, closing conference: CIA term: closing communication, also called an exit conference; it may be held.
key_terminologies.Management response: CIA term: action plan, with a named owner and a target date.
key_terminologies.Follow-up activities: CIA wording: Standard 15.2 Confirming the Implementation of Recommendations or Action Plans; 'follow-up' stays in ordinary use.
key_terminologies.ISACA Code of Professional Ethics: CIA counterpart: Domain II of the Standards, Ethics and Professionalism, Principles 1 to 5. The Standards call The IIA's earlier code the former Code of Ethics.
key_terminologies.ITAF standards and guidelines: CIA counterpart: the Global Internal Audit Standards (Requirements and Considerations for Implementation), Topical Requirements and Global Guidance, cited as Standard 9.4 and so on.
key_terminologies.Quality assurance of the audit function,: CIA terms: quality assurance and improvement program; external quality assessment.
key_terminologies.Advisory (consulting) engagement: CIA term: advisory services. The Standards' glossary records consulting services as the older name.
key_terminologies.Self-review threat: CIA terms: impairment to objectivity; self-review bias and familiarity bias.
